newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek bankers want to know more about 5-yr bond. [CORRECTED 13:40 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Greek bankers want to know more about 5-yr bond. [CORRECTED 13:40 GMT]

text.p: Greece is going to auction its first five-year fixed coupon bond next week and bankers want the treasury to announce the basic terms of the issue and clarify its position on the retroactive taxation of outstanding FRNs.
"We are eager to hear the specific terms of the bond issue and have the government's official position on the retroactive taxation issue of old FRNs," said a senior banker at a foreign bank.

Deputy Finance Minister Nikos Christodoulakis told reporters on Monday that Greece would issue a fixed coupon five-year bond and 7-year FRNs next week but did not disclose information about coupon, bank commissions and its taxation status.

"We are familiar with FRN auctions so it does not really matter whether the treasury provides the information well in advance but it is a different ball game for the fixed-coupon bond," said another senior dealer at a foreign bank.

Because the finance ministry has been tight-lipped, there has been market speculation that the finance ministry might not auction the much-awaited five-year issue due to a liquidity squeeze in the interbank market.
Other speculation had the finance ministry proceeding with a private placement of seven-year FRNs or fixed-coupon bonds.

"The finance ministry has to understand that uncertainty regarding taxation and other matters pertaining to the auction of five-year bonds will not help it get the highest (Corrects from lowest) possible bids," another banker said.
Many dealers told Reuters there would be strong demand for the fixed-coupon bond if the government ruled out retroactive taxation of outstanding FRNs.
The prevailing market view is that the government will not tax the outstanding FRNs retroactively but the government has yet to clarify its position in public.

There has been a great deal of market speculation on the taxation issue partly because the 1997 budget is due this month and it is clear the government considering various new taxes to raise revenues.

An informal market survey by Reuters showed dealers expected the average yield to range between 10.75 and 12.50 percent for the five-year issue, with foreign investors on the upper side of expectations.
"I am not interested if the yield is below 12 percent," said a London-based bond trader. "In my view, Greece's credit rating does not justify a lower yield right now."
Greece's foreign debt has been put on credit watch for a possible upgrade, Moody's investors services said in a statement last week. Greek domestic debt is not rated.

Some dealers said eurobonds issued by the Hellenic Republic with five years left to maturity were priced about 50 basis points above the six-month Libor which produced an average yield of 11 percent or more on the five-year fixed coupon bond via cross-currency swaps.
Greek press reports have said the treasury could set the coupon somewhere between 10 and 11 percent.
Some bankers criticised of finance ministry for not auctioning a fixed-coupon bond in October when market conditions were better.
"Markets do not wait for you to make up your mind. Officials at the treasury have to learn to act fast and take advantage of good market conditions," said a senior banker.
The next regular meeting of a new committee set up to manage Greece's public debt is on November 25. -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
